plan.contextChunk: This figure shows two orbital drawings of a carbon-carbon double bond separated by a labeled arrow, before and after a twist. On the left, two carbons lettered "C" are stacked diagonally, each drawn with a pink lobe above and a blue lobe below, the lobes tapering to points at the carbon and each pink lobe carrying a small black dot. The two sets are parallel, and thin straight lines run along the outer edges of the upper pink pair and the lower blue pair to show that the lobes line up so their broad faces overlap sideways; short black bars and dashed lines at each carbon mark the remaining bonds and the plane they occupy. A horizontal arrow across the middle is labeled "rotate 90°". On the right the lower carbon is unchanged, but the upper one has been turned so its pink lobe points toward the viewer at the left and its blue lobe away at the right, leaving the two pairs crossing at right angles instead of running parallel. Bold labels beneath read "π bond (p orbitals are parallel)" and "Broken π bond after rotation (p orbitals are perpendicular)". Setting the aligned lobes against the crossed ones makes sideways overlap the thing to watch, explaining why twisting such a bond costs the full strength of the pi bond and so does not happen freely.

elements: lower carbon nucleus (small sphere) with 'C' label
upper carbon nucleus (small sphere) with 'C' label
lower p orbital: pink teardrop lobe pointing up-left and blue teardrop lobe pointing down-right, both tapering to the nucleus, lying in the screen plane
upper p orbital: pink and blue teardrop lobes that rotate rigidly about the C=C axis from parallel (0°) to perpendicular (90°)
small black electron dot centered in each pink lobe (upper dot rotates with its lobe)
two short black sigma-bond rods at each carbon, splayed trigonally in each carbon's plane (upper pair rotates with the upper carbon)
dashed reference line through each carbon marking its trigonal plane edge-on (upper one rotates with the twist)
two thin dark bracket lines running along the outer edges of the pink-lobe pair and the blue-lobe pair, showing the lobes are parallel (visible only near 0°)
translucent amber overlap glow between the facing pink lobes and between the facing blue lobes, fading with twist angle
π-bond overlap gauge (HUD bar) showing strength = cos(angle)
state caption: 'π bond (p orbitals are parallel)' / 'Broken π bond after rotation (p orbitals are perpendicular)'

interactions.label: Rotation angle about C=C
interactions.teaches: Twisting one carbon about the double bond progressively destroys the sideways overlap of the p orbitals — π-bond strength falls as cos(angle) and reaches zero at 90°, which is why rotation about a double bond is not free

interactions.label: Bond state
interactions.teaches: The two endpoint configurations share the same unmoved carbon framework — only the orbital orientation changes, so sideways overlap exists exclusively when the p orbitals are parallel
At 90° the upper pink lobe points toward the viewer and the blue lobe away — orbiting reveals the true 3D perpendicularity that the flat drawing can only suggest

demo_steps.title: Aligned p orbitals (π bond intact)
demo_steps.narration: At 0° the pink and blue lobes on both carbons line up, bracket lines show their broad faces overlapping sideways, and the overlap gauge reads its maximum (cos 0° = 1).

demo_steps.title: Twisting weakens the π bond
demo_steps.narration: At 45° the upper orbital has swung halfway around; the bracket lines and overlap glow fade and the gauge drops to cos 45° ≈ 0.71 — the lobes no longer face each other squarely.

demo_steps.title: 90° twist — π bond broken
demo_steps.narration: At 90° the p orbitals are perpendicular: the upper pink lobe points toward you, the blue one away. The gauge reads zero — sideways overlap is gone, so a full twist costs the entire π-bond strength.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: C=C axis tilted ~30° from vertical in the screen plane (z=0), running lower-left to upper-right as in the source: axis direction d=(0.5, 0.866, 0), carbons at ±1.25·d, i.e. lower C at (-0.62, -1.08, 0) and upper C at (+0.62, +1.08, 0), nucleus spheres r≈0.12, dark gray #2b2b2b, each with a bold black 'C' label sprite beside it. Each p-orbital lobe is a teardrop ~1.15 long, max radius ~0.55, tip at its nucleus. At 0° both orbitals lie along the in-screen perpendicular p0=(-0.866, 0.5, 0): pink lobe up-left, blue lobe down-right (both carbons parallel, matching the left panel). The upper carbon's ENTIRE group (both lobes, its electron dot, its two sigma rods, its dashed plane line) rotates rigidly about the C=C axis d by the slider angle; at 90° its pink lobe points toward +Z (viewer) and blue toward -Z, matching the right panel. Pink lobes #ef6f8e, blue lobes #4e7fbf, slightly glossy and ~90% opaque. Black electron dots r≈0.07 (#111) at pink-lobe centroids (~0.6 from nucleus along the lobe axis). Sigma rods: black cylinders r≈0.05, length ~0.8, at each carbon in its trigonal plane pointing away from the other carbon, splayed ±55° from the C=C direction. Dashed lines through each carbon along its in-plane perpendicular (±p0 direction for lower carbon; rotated for upper), length ~1.6, gray #666. Bracket lines: thin (#333, r≈0.015) lines parallel to the C=C axis, one offset beyond the pink lobes' outer edges, one beyond the blue lobes', length ~3.6; fade opacity linearly to 0 by θ=30°. Overlap glow: amber (#f2b544) translucent ellipsoids between the two pink lobes and the two blue lobes, opacity = 0.35·cosθ. Overlap gauge: horizontal HUD bar, fill fraction = cos(θ), labeled 'π-bond overlap ∝ cos θ'. Overall scene spans x ∈ [-2.2, 2.2], y ∈ [-2.4, 2.4]. White background.
interactionPlan.notes: Build lobes with LatheGeometry using a teardrop profile (or spheres scaled ~2:1 with a cone taper) and MeshStandardMaterial with roughness ~0.35. Parent the upper carbon's lobes, dot, sigma rods, and dashed line into one Group and rotate that group about the C=C axis vector (use quaternion setFromAxisAngle with axis d) so everything stays rigid. The toggle snaps the slider to 0 or 90; moving the slider off the endpoints leaves the toggle in a neutral/indeterminate visual state. Update bracket-line opacity, glow opacity, gauge fill, and caption text reactively each frame from θ (gauge and glow strictly follow cosθ; caption switches at θ < 45 vs ≥ 45). Use HTML/CSS or sprite text for 'C' labels, gauge, and caption so they stay legible; keep lighting soft (hemisphere + key light) to preserve the textbook's pastel look.

authoredContext:
Although essentially free rotation around single bonds is possible (another section), the same is not true of double bonds. For rotation to occur around a double bond, the π bond must break and re-form (the figure). Thus, the barrier to double-bond rotation must be at least as great as the strength of the π bond itself, an estimated 350 kJ/mol (84 kcal/mol). Recall that the barrier to bond rotation in ethane is only 12 kJ/mol.

The π bond must break for rotation to take place around a carbon–carbon double bond.

An orbital diagram with two parallel p orbitals before rotation. After rotation the p orbitals are perpendicular, which breaks the double bond.

The lack of rotation around carbon–carbon double bonds is of more than just theoretical interest; it also has chemical consequences. Imagine the situation for a disubstituted alkene such as 2-butene. (Disubstituted means that two substituents other than hydrogen are bonded to the double-bond carbons.) The two methyl groups in 2-butene can either be on the same side of the double bond or on opposite sides, a situation similar to that in disubstituted cycloalkanes (another section).

plan.contextChunk: This figure shows two orbital drawings of a carbon-carbon double bond separated by a labeled arrow, before and after a twist. On the left, two carbons lettered "C" are stacked diagonally, each drawn with a pink lobe above and a blue lobe below, the lobes tapering to points at the carbon and each pink lobe carrying a small black dot. The two sets are parallel, and thin straight lines run along the outer edges of the upper pink pair and the lower blue pair to show that the lobes line up so their broad faces overlap sideways; short black bars and dashed lines at each carbon mark the remaining bonds and the plane they occupy. A horizontal arrow across the middle is labeled "rotate 90°". On the right the lower carbon is unchanged, but the upper one has been turned so its pink lobe points toward the viewer at the left and its blue lobe away at the right, leaving the two pairs crossing at right angles instead of running parallel. Bold labels beneath read "π bond (p orbitals are parallel)" and "Broken π bond after rotation (p orbitals are perpendicular)". Setting the aligned lobes against the crossed ones makes sideways overlap the thing to watch, explaining why twisting such a bond costs the full strength of the pi bond and so does not happen freely.

elements: lower carbon nucleus (small sphere) with 'C' label
upper carbon nucleus (small sphere) with 'C' label
lower p orbital: pink teardrop lobe pointing up-left and blue teardrop lobe pointing down-right, both tapering to the nucleus, lying in the screen plane
upper p orbital: pink and blue teardrop lobes that rotate rigidly about the C=C axis from parallel (0°) to perpendicular (90°)
small black electron dot centered in each pink lobe (upper dot rotates with its lobe)
two short black sigma-bond rods at each carbon, splayed trigonally in each carbon's plane (upper pair rotates with the upper carbon)
dashed reference line through each carbon marking its trigonal plane edge-on (upper one rotates with the twist)
two thin dark bracket lines running along the outer edges of the pink-lobe pair and the blue-lobe pair, showing the lobes are parallel (visible only near 0°)
translucent amber overlap glow between the facing pink lobes and between the facing blue lobes, fading with twist angle
π-bond overlap gauge (HUD bar) showing strength = cos(angle)
state caption: 'π bond (p orbitals are parallel)' / 'Broken π bond after rotation (p orbitals are perpendicular)'

interactions.label: Rotation angle about C=C
interactions.teaches: Twisting one carbon about the double bond progressively destroys the sideways overlap of the p orbitals — π-bond strength falls as cos(angle) and reaches zero at 90°, which is why rotation about a double bond is not free

interactions.label: Bond state
interactions.teaches: The two endpoint configurations share the same unmoved carbon framework — only the orbital orientation changes, so sideways overlap exists exclusively when the p orbitals are parallel
At 90° the upper pink lobe points toward the viewer and the blue lobe away — orbiting reveals the true 3D perpendicularity that the flat drawing can only suggest

demo_steps.title: Aligned p orbitals (π bond intact)
demo_steps.narration: At 0° the pink and blue lobes on both carbons line up, bracket lines show their broad faces overlapping sideways, and the overlap gauge reads its maximum (cos 0° = 1).

demo_steps.title: Twisting weakens the π bond
demo_steps.narration: At 45° the upper orbital has swung halfway around; the bracket lines and overlap glow fade and the gauge drops to cos 45° ≈ 0.71 — the lobes no longer face each other squarely.

demo_steps.title: 90° twist — π bond broken
demo_steps.narration: At 90° the p orbitals are perpendicular: the upper pink lobe points toward you, the blue one away. The gauge reads zero — sideways overlap is gone, so a full twist costs the entire π-bond strength.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: C=C axis tilted ~30° from vertical in the screen plane (z=0), running lower-left to upper-right as in the source: axis direction d=(0.5, 0.866, 0), carbons at ±1.25·d, i.e. lower C at (-0.62, -1.08, 0) and upper C at (+0.62, +1.08, 0), nucleus spheres r≈0.12, dark gray #2b2b2b, each with a bold black 'C' label sprite beside it. Each p-orbital lobe is a teardrop ~1.15 long, max radius ~0.55, tip at its nucleus. At 0° both orbitals lie along the in-screen perpendicular p0=(-0.866, 0.5, 0): pink lobe up-left, blue lobe down-right (both carbons parallel, matching the left panel). The upper carbon's ENTIRE group (both lobes, its electron dot, its two sigma rods, its dashed plane line) rotates rigidly about the C=C axis d by the slider angle; at 90° its pink lobe points toward +Z (viewer) and blue toward -Z, matching the right panel. Pink lobes #ef6f8e, blue lobes #4e7fbf, slightly glossy and ~90% opaque. Black electron dots r≈0.07 (#111) at pink-lobe centroids (~0.6 from nucleus along the lobe axis). Sigma rods: black cylinders r≈0.05, length ~0.8, at each carbon in its trigonal plane pointing away from the other carbon, splayed ±55° from the C=C direction. Dashed lines through each carbon along its in-plane perpendicular (±p0 direction for lower carbon; rotated for upper), length ~1.6, gray #666. Bracket lines: thin (#333, r≈0.015) lines parallel to the C=C axis, one offset beyond the pink lobes' outer edges, one beyond the blue lobes', length ~3.6; fade opacity linearly to 0 by θ=30°. Overlap glow: amber (#f2b544) translucent ellipsoids between the two pink lobes and the two blue lobes, opacity = 0.35·cosθ. Overlap gauge: horizontal HUD bar, fill fraction = cos(θ), labeled 'π-bond overlap ∝ cos θ'. Overall scene spans x ∈ [-2.2, 2.2], y ∈ [-2.4, 2.4]. White background.
interactionPlan.notes: Build lobes with LatheGeometry using a teardrop profile (or spheres scaled ~2:1 with a cone taper) and MeshStandardMaterial with roughness ~0.35. Parent the upper carbon's lobes, dot, sigma rods, and dashed line into one Group and rotate that group about the C=C axis vector (use quaternion setFromAxisAngle with axis d) so everything stays rigid. The toggle snaps the slider to 0 or 90; moving the slider off the endpoints leaves the toggle in a neutral/indeterminate visual state. Update bracket-line opacity, glow opacity, gauge fill, and caption text reactively each frame from θ (gauge and glow strictly follow cosθ; caption switches at θ < 45 vs ≥ 45). Use HTML/CSS or sprite text for 'C' labels, gauge, and caption so they stay legible; keep lighting soft (hemisphere + key light) to preserve the textbook's pastel look.
